agentResponses.content:
**First, a quarrel with "adapt."** The word does a lot of quiet work. It presumes the product is essentially correct and only its surface is foreign — that there's a translation layer, a localisation budget, a sprint or two of currency symbols and local names in the word problems. Sometimes that's true. More often what's being proposed is a second product with the first one's brand on it, and the difference matters enormously, because one of those things can be run by a localisation manager and the other needs a person with the authority to break the roadmap.

And **"well-received" by whom?** K-12 has at least four customers who are not the same person and frequently want opposite things: the ministry or state that approves, the district or school that pays, the teacher who is inconvenienced, and the parent who is anxious. In our current markets those roles may be collapsed or familiar enough that we've stopped noticing them. In the new one they may sit in four different buildings with four different fiscal calendars. A product beloved by teachers and unpurchasable is a hobby. A product procured centrally and quietly unused for three years is worse — it's a renewal that doesn't come and a reference that turns negative.

Someone should say out loud, before anything else, **which of those four we're actually building for in year one**, because the answers produce different products, not different go-to-market plans.

---

**The gravitational body: the exam.**

In most systems that aren't ours, there is a high-stakes examination that functions as the actual curriculum regardless of what the official curriculum document says. It determines what teachers teach, what parents pay for, what students believe learning is, and what counts as a legitimate educational activity. Everything in orbit around it gets funded. Everything outside that orbit is enrichment, and enrichment is bought with a hobby budget by the schools that need us least.

So the first piece of real work is unglamorous: **acquire the last five years of the examination papers, the official syllabus documents, and the three best-selling local revision workbooks, and diff them against our scope and sequence, item by item.** Not to see whether we "align" — we won't — but to find out *how* we misalign. There are three very different failure modes and they have different costs:

- **Ordering.** We teach the right things in the wrong grade. Cheap. Re-sequence.
- **Coverage.** There are topics we simply don't have, and topics we have that nobody there needs. Moderate. Commission and cut.
- **Epistemology.** What counts as a correct answer, a valid method, a good explanation, is different. Expensive, and usually discovered late and by accident.

That third one is where naive entrants die. Division notation differs. The long-division algorithm differs. The decimal separator differs. Whether showing work is mandatory differs. Whether a student is expected to produce the method taught or any method that works differs — and that is a pedagogical value dressed as a marking rule. Our adaptive engine's "wrong answer" logic encodes assumptions no one has ever written down, because in our home market they were simply the water.

**Sensitivities, said plainly and once:** evolution, human reproduction, cosmology and origins, national history and its contested episodes, religious content, gender representation, borders on maps. Every one of these is somebody's line, and the lines are not where we'd guess. Content review by locals with actual authority to strike material, before launch, not after a screenshot circulates.

---

**Pedagogy: the assumption stack nobody documents.**

Our product almost certainly assumes: one device per learner, learner-paced progression, work continued at home, the teacher as facilitator, formative assessment without grades, choice as motivating, and a certain comfort with productive struggle and visible failure.

The new system may run on: whole-class instruction at a single pace, teacher as unquestioned authority and knowledge source, one projector or none, 45–55 students, shared or no devices, homework as paper, ranked and published scores as the normal and expected feedback mechanism, and a strong cultural preference for accuracy over exploration.

Note that these aren't deficits to be corrected. That framing is the whole disease. **Every "modernising" edtech entry that positions itself as bringing better pedagogy to a backward system loses to a local company selling exam questions.** Reliably. It loses because it asks teachers to change their practice *first* and receive the benefit *later*, and no teacher with 52 students and a public pass-rate target takes that trade.

So: **a hard filter for the entire feature set. No feature ships into this market if the teacher has to change their practice before they get the benefit.** Benefit first, behaviour change second, and only if they want it. This kills a surprising amount of the roadmap and it should.

What survives the filter is not glamorous:

*The unit of delivery becomes the lesson, not the learner.* A projector-first mode. One screen, front of room, teacher-driven, works with zero student devices. This feels like a regression to our product team and is very likely the single highest-leverage build in the programme, because it is the only form of the product that fits the room as it actually exists.

*Marking, prep, and reporting.* The teacher's binding constraint is labour, not capability. Item banks that generate differentiated practice they'd otherwise write by hand. Auto-marking that produces the report format the *ministry* wants, in the ministry's own template. Whatever administrative artefact they currently produce at 11pm on Sundays — produce it for them. That's the wedge. It requires no pedagogical conversion and it buys us the right to be in the building.

*Print as a first-class output.* Every worksheet, every practice set, exportable to paper, formatted for local paper sizes, legible on a bad photocopier. And — I'd say this quietly and mean it seriously — **if our materials start getting photocopied and shared without licence, that is the most encouraging data we will receive all year.** It is unmet demand with a distribution mechanism attached. Metering it is a later problem and a nice one to have.

*Offline-first, and I mean architecturally, not as a sync feature.* Content packs that live on the device or a local server. Assume intermittent connectivity, metered data that the *teacher personally pays for*, low-end Android, 2GB RAM, small screens. Measure our payload in megabytes and treat it as a headline metric. A 40MB lesson is a lesson that doesn't happen.

*And the identity model, which is where a lot of platforms quietly break.* Per-student accounts assume per-student devices. Shared devices, shared logins, siblings on one phone, a class of 50 rotating through six tablets — our data model may simply have no way to represent this, and if it can't, then our analytics, our adaptivity, and our reporting are all producing confident nonsense. Worth checking early, because it's a schema problem and schema problems are never small.

---

**What is actually our asset? Because it isn't the content.**

Worth being clinical here. Content is local, perishable, politically constrained, and — in a market with an established textbook publishing industry and a shadow-education sector — already produced better and cheaper than we can. The portable asset is more likely the delivery infrastructure, the assessment engine, the item-generation and adaptivity, the teacher workflow, the reporting.

If that's right, the entry strategy is not "translate our library." It's **licence, commission, or acquire local content and run it through our engine** — ideally in partnership with an incumbent who already has curriculum legitimacy, distribution into schools, and a relationship with the approvals body. A local textbook publisher has everything we lack and lacks everything we have. That conversation is worth having before the build, not after the first disappointing quarter.

Which surfaces the uncomfortable engineering question underneath all of this: **can our codebase separate content from pedagogy from delivery?** If curriculum structure, grade levels, assessment logic, and sequencing are hard-coded — and in most platforms built for a single market, they are, because why wouldn't they be — then this market entry is a refactor wearing an international-expansion costume, and it should be budgeted, staffed, and *timed* as a refactor. The cost of the second country is mostly paid during the first one. The cost of the third is nearly zero if we do this properly and nearly identical to the second if we don't. That's the real decision hiding in here, and it's an architecture decision being made by a commercial committee.

---

**Money, and the awkward arithmetic.**

Willingness to pay may be a fifth of home, or a twentieth. Per-seat SaaS may be structurally impossible against a public school budget that has no line item for software. So:

- **Who has money?** Often not schools. Often parents, and specifically parents buying exam preparation, which is a consumer business with consumer economics and consumer churn and nothing whatever to do with our current motion.
- **Public procurement** operates on tender cycles, fiscal years, local-entity requirements, and possibly a mandated local partner. It is slow, large, reference-driven, and politically reversible with a change of minister. Worth pursuing; unwise to depend on.
- **Distribution rails that already exist:** telco bundling and zero-rated data, device OEM preloads, textbook adoption, tuition-centre chains, teacher associations. Each of these has a gatekeeper who is easier to convince than 30,000 schools.
- **Data residency and children's privacy law** will likely require in-country hosting and may forbid several things our analytics currently do by default. This is a build cost and a legal cost, and it's cheaper to discover in month one than in month fourteen.

---

**People, which is the part that's usually decided badly and early.**

Not an expatriate general manager with the playbook. Someone with genuine standing inside that education system — a former ministry official, a respected head teacher, a curriculum author — hired early, paid properly, and given something most companies won't give:

**Veto power over the global roadmap for their market.** If they can't say no to headquarters, we are not entering a market, we are exporting into one and calling it entry. The test is simple and it will happen within four months: they will ask for something that looks parochial and unscalable, our platform team will explain why it's not a priority, and whoever wins that argument determines the outcome of the entire programme. Better to settle who wins it now, in writing, while it's abstract.

**And the compensation point, which matters more than the strategy document.** Whoever runs year one should not be paid on seats or revenue. Pay them on evidence — validated curriculum alignment, teacher retention through a full term, one publicly citable reference school, an honest account of what doesn't work. Because a person paid on seats will sell a hundred district pilots that nobody uses, book them as traction, and the truth will arrive eighteen months later with a renewal rate attached. Policy is what we write; comp is what we actually asked for.

---

**Cheap ways to find out whether any of this is true, this term.**

- **Put the current product, entirely unchanged, in front of fifteen local teachers and watch where they stop.** Don't explain it. Don't guide. The first eight friction points will be things no one in the building has thought about, and it costs almost nothing. Film it if they'll let us.
- **Buy the three best-selling revision workbooks and the top-grossing local app.** That's the competitive set. Not other platforms — the shadow-education market. Read what they actually promise. It will be scores, and it will be scores stated numerically.
- **Run the product with no product.** A concierge cohort — one class, one teacher, materials delivered by whatever messaging app the country actually lives in, marking done by a human on our side. Learn what's wanted before building the machine that delivers it. If nobody wants the manual version, the automated version has no audience either.
- **Instrument reality.** Actual bandwidth, actual devices, actual screen sizes, actual electricity, in three schools of different types — urban private, urban public, rural public. The national statistics will flatter us.
- **Interview the approvals path.** Find out who must say yes, how long they take, and what has recently been rejected and why. Rejections are more informative than approvals and are usually public.
- **Diff the exam.** Already mentioned. It's the single highest-value week of work available and it can begin tomorrow with a credit card and a translator.
- **Pre-commit the definition of activation, in writing, before the first pilot.** A logged-in student is not a used product. Everyone discovers a generous definition of engagement once the board deck is due, and I'd rather we choose our self-deception deliberately than stumble into it.

Cheap, parallel, mostly negative results. Two of them will change the plan materially, and I couldn't reliably tell you which two, which is rather the point of running them all.

---

**Sequencing.**

Narrow, dull, and exam-adjacent first. One subject, one or two grade bands, the ones nearest the high-stakes examination, in a handful of schools where we can be physically present. Teacher-workflow value before student-facing value. Projector mode before 1:1. Print export before adaptivity. A local reference name before any advertising. A second subject only after a full term's retention data — a full *term*, because the term is the real unit of truth in schools and everything looks wonderful in week three.

The pedagogical ambitions — inquiry, personalisation, student agency, the things we'd genuinely argue are better — go last, offered as an option to the minority of schools that ask, never as the premise. If we're right about them, we'll be invited. If we lead with them, we'll be a foreign company that arrived to tell teachers they'd been doing it wrong, and no amount of subsequent humility undoes that first impression.

---

**One question I'd leave with the board, since it isn't mine to settle.**

Is this a market entry or a product decision? Because if the honest answer is that succeeding here requires a differently-shaped product, sold to a different buyer, at a different price, through different rails, with locally authored content — then what exactly are we exporting? Possibly the brand, possibly the engine, possibly only the capital. All three are legitimate answers. They imply completely different organisational structures, and the choice between them stops being reversible at around month five, at which point it will look like a series of small technical decisions rather than the strategic commitment it actually was.

There's also a version of this where the most valuable output isn't the new market at all — it's the internal capability to enter the *next* one in nine months instead of three years. That's an argument for spending more on architecture and less on launch, and it's an argument that never wins on its own merits because the return arrives one country later than the person making the case.

I'd want that debate had before the first commitment rather than after. Meanwhile, the exam diff and the fifteen unguided teacher sessions require nobody's permission and about three weeks. One of them will tell us whether we're localising a product or building one.
